aspects.says: Input is decoded and normalised the way the next layer will, then the whole canonical string is matched against an allow-list, and the canonical value is passed on.
basis: section:Validate the Value the Next Layer Will Use, Against an Allow-List

aspects.says: A deny-list compares characters as typed, so percent-encoded and full-width spellings pass it and become the forbidden text one layer later.
basis: section:Validate the Value the Next Layer Will Use, Against an Allow-List

aspects.says: NFKC folds full-width forms into ASCII but leaves look-alike letters of other scripts unchanged; only the allow-list's character range refuses them.
basis: section:Validate the Value the Next Layer Will Use, Against an Allow-List

aspects.says: An overridden toString protects one record; another record holding the same values as Strings prints them again, while a Secret type carries the mask with the value.
basis: section:A Record's toString Prints Every Component, Password Included

aspects.says: java.util.Random is a fixed formula of a 48-bit seed; a clock seed repeats tokens and leaving the seed out still leaves it not cryptographically secure.
basis: section:A Token from Random Is a Function of Its Seed; Use SecureRandom

aspects.says: A record's generated toString prints every component, so log calls, exception messages and enclosing records print a password component.
basis: section:A Record's toString Prints Every Component, Password Included

aspects.says: A redacting toString keeps the non-secret components and shows nothing of the secret, so an enclosing record's generated toString is safe too.
basis: section:A Record's toString Prints Every Component, Password Included

aspects.says: The SecurityManager is deprecated for removal (JEP 411); on Java 21 setSecurityManager throws UnsupportedOperationException unless java.security.manager=allow.
basis: section:10.6.1. Security Best Practices in Java
aspects.reason: a one-clause note on the platform's history; nothing the reader writes depends on it, and the practices run on a later JDK where it behaves differently

aspects.says: A SHA1PRNG seeded before its first use repeats its output for the same seed, while NativePRNG mixes a seed into its own state.
basis: section:A Token from Random Is a Function of Its Seed; Use SecureRandom

aspects.says: Wiping a char[] removes that array's copy, but a String made from it cannot be overwritten and stays in the heap, and in a whole-heap dump, until a collection reclaims it.
basis: section:Wiping a char[] Removes Your Copy of a Secret; a String Copy Stays Until GC

aspects.says: A secret held in char[] is wiped in a finally block, in the caller's array and in every copy the code made.
basis: section:Wiping a char[] Removes Your Copy of a Secret; a String Copy Stays Until GC
